spatial_claims.claim: A and B are endpoints of the given arc, lying on the circle
AB is a chord; D is the midpoint of AB, so AD = DB; D lies on segment AB
D is an interior point of the circle (since chord AB lies within the circle by 3.2)
Perpendicular to AB at D is drawn toward the given arc, meeting the arc at C
C is on the given arc (on the circle)
Triangles ADC and BDC share side DC, with AD = DB and angles ADC = BDC = 90 degrees (SAS configuration)
By I.4 (SAS), angle DAC = angle DBC
D lies between A and B on segment AB, so ray AD = ray AB and ray BD = ray BA
Angle DAC coincides with angle BAC; angle DBC coincides with angle ABC
Inscribed angle BAC at vertex A stands on arc BC (not containing A); inscribed angle ABC at vertex B stands on arc AC (not containing B)
By 3.26, equal inscribed angles in the same circle subtend equal arcs, so arc BC = arc AC

configuration_map: Points A and B are the endpoints of the given arc, both on the circle. D is the midpoint of chord AB, lying on segment AB and hence interior to the circle. C is the point where the perpendicular to AB at D (directed toward the given arc) meets the arc, so C is on the circle between A and B along the given arc. Triangles ADC and BDC share the perpendicular segment DC, with AD = DB and right angles at D. Throughout the proof, D remains on segment AB (interior to the circle), and C remains on the given arc. The angles BAC and ABC are inscribed angles in the circle at vertices A and B respectively, subtending arcs BC and AC (the two portions of the given arc separated by C).
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The configuration is straightforward: perpendicular from midpoint of chord to arc. D's position on segment AB correctly implies ray coincidences (DAC=BAC, DBC=ABC). The SAS congruence is standard. The application of 3.26 to equal inscribed angles yielding equal arcs is geometrically valid. No angle decomposition issues, no inside/outside contradictions, no betweenness conflicts.
